topic: Control flow: if, when, ranges & loops

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `if` is an expression: each branch is a block whose last expression becomes the value, so `label` is `"O"`. The `println("odd")` still runs as a side effect before the value is produced, so both lines are printed.

questions.question: What happens when you compile this line?
options: Compile error: an `if` expression needs an `else` branch
It compiles and `max` is `Int?`, `null` when `a <= b`
It compiles and `max` is `Unit` when `a <= b`
It compiles but throws IllegalStateException at runtime when `a <= b`
questions.explanation: When `if` is used as an expression its value must exist on every path, so Kotlin requires an `else`. It never silently produces `null` or `Unit`; only an `if` used as a statement may omit `else`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `1 until 4` and `1..<4` are both half-open ranges that exclude the end, while `1..4` includes it. `..<` is just the operator form of `until`.

questions.question: True or false: this loop prints `54321`.
questions.explanation: `..` always counts upward, so `5..1` is an empty range and the loop body never runs. To count down you need `5 downTo 1`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `200, 201 ->` matches either value, `in 400..499` is a range check and `!in 0..599` matches values outside the range. `302` is inside `0..599` so it falls to `else`, while `700` is outside and hits the `!in` branch.

questions.question: In this Activity menu handler, why is the `else` branch required?
options: `when` is an expression on an `Int`, and an `Int` subject can't be exhaustive without `else`
`R.id` values aren't compile-time constants, and `when` needs `else` for non-constant branches
Without `else` the matching branch would fall through into the next one
questions.explanation: The `when` is the return value, so it must produce a `Boolean` for every possible `itemId`, which only `else` can guarantee for an `Int`. Branch conditions don't need to be constants, and Kotlin's `when` never falls through.

questions.question: True or false: `repeat(3) { print(it) }` prints `012`.
questions.explanation: `repeat(n)` calls the lambda `n` times and passes the zero-based iteration index as `it`, so it prints `0`, `1`, `2`. It does not start at 1.

questions.question: Which of these produce exactly the sequence `10, 8, 6, 4, 2`? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `downTo` counts down and `step` takes a positive step size, and `reversed()` flips a progression, so the first three all give `10, 8, 6, 4, 2`. `10..2` is an empty range, and a negative `step` throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `withIndex()` gives `(index, value)` pairs you can destructure, and `lastIndex` is `size - 1`, so there's no trailing `|`. `indices` is `0..2`, and `reversed()` makes it count down from `2`.

questions.question: What happens with this code?
options: Compile error: the `when` expression is not exhaustive
questions.explanation: A `when` used as an expression over an enum must cover every constant or have an `else`, and `SYSTEM` is missing, so the compiler rejects it. Kotlin checks this at compile time instead of failing at runtime.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `while` checks its condition before the first iteration, so with `a = 10` its body never runs. `do-while` checks after the body, so it always runs at least once and prints `d10 ` before the check fails.

questions.question: What happens with this code?
options: Compile error: `code` is only in scope inside the `when`
Compile error: you can't declare a `val` inside `when (...)`
questions.explanation: `when (val code = fetchCode())` is allowed, but `code` is scoped to the `when` body only. That's the point of the syntax: it keeps the captured value from leaking into the surrounding scope, so the last `println(code)` doesn't compile.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Destructuring a `Map.Entry` gives `(key, value)`, and `mapOf` keeps insertion order. `continue` skips only the current entry (`pear`), so iteration goes on to `fig` instead of stopping.

questions.question: True or false: this compiles, because a `when` used as a statement doesn't need to be exhaustive.
questions.explanation: Since Kotlin 1.7, a `when` statement whose subject is a `Boolean`, enum or sealed type must be exhaustive too, so this needs a `false` or `else` branch. Only statements over other types (like `Int` or `String`) may skip cases.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `'a'..'k'` is a `CharRange`, and `step 3` keeps `a, d, g, j`. `k` is not reached, so the progression's `last` is `j`, not the range's end `k`.

questions.question: A teammate adds `object Empty : UiState`. What happens to `render`?
options: It stops compiling until `Empty` is handled
It compiles, and `Empty` is silently ignored
It compiles but throws `NoWhenBranchMatchedException` when `Empty` arrives
It compiles with only a warning
questions.explanation: Because `when` is used as an expression with no `else`, the compiler checks that it covers every subtype of the sealed interface. A new subtype breaks the build, which is why teams leave out `else` for UI state.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `continue@outer` abandons the inner loop and moves to the next `i`, so `j = 3` is never reached. When `i == 3`, `break@outer` exits both loops before printing `31`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A bare `return` inside `forEach` returns from the enclosing function `first()`, so the loop stops at `2`. `return@forEach` only ends the current lambda call, so it works like `continue` and `3` is still printed.

questions.question: What happens when this runs?
options: It prints `abc`, because `0..items.size` stops at the last index
It prints `ab`, since `..` excludes the upper bound
questions.explanation: `0..items.size` is inclusive, so it reaches index `3` on a list of size 3. Use `items.indices` or `0 until items.size` (`0..<items.size`) instead.

questions.question: Which statements about `when` are true? Select all that apply.
options: With a subject, branch conditions can be any expression, such as a function call, not just constants
Only the first matching branch runs; there is no fall-through
An `is` branch smart-casts the subject inside that branch
With a subject `x: Int`, a branch `x > 5 ->` checks whether `x` is greater than 5
A `when` without a subject always needs an `else`, even as a statement
questions.explanation: With a subject, each branch value is compared to the subject, so `x > 5` would compare the `Int` against a `Boolean` and the compiler rejects it. Use a subject-less `when { x > 5 -> ... }` for that. A subject-less `when` used as a statement doesn't need `else`.
